patient.chief_complaint: Sudden left arm weakness and sensory changes — 3 hours after insulin dose
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. K is a 24-year-old final-year undergraduate with Type 1 diabetes on an insulin pump and celiac disease who presents with 3-hour history of sudden left arm weakness and hemisensory loss. She received a regular insulin bolus 3 hours ago. Her thesis defense was rejected for resubmission 2 weeks ago, creating significant stress. She is otherwise healthy and her diabetes has been well-controlled. She has celiac disease managed with gluten-free diet. The clinical puzzle in this case has multiple layers: (1) Insulin therapy → immediate glucose check mandatory to exclude hypoglycemia; (2) Type 1 diabetes → cerebrovascular risk factor (though modest at age 24); (3) Celiac disease → neurological complications are real (gluten ataxia, celiac neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration from B12 malabsorption). The arm drift sign (arm drifting UPWARD rather than downward) is the pathognomonic positive FND sign that experienced clinicians recognize as impossible in organic hemiparesis. However, this sign requires confirmation after glucose normalization and celiac neurological complications are excluded.

findings.finding: ARM DRIFT TEST: Left arm placed at 90 degrees horizontal. Over 10 seconds: LEFT ARM DRIFTS UPWARD (toward ceiling) rather than downward. Organic UMN weakness causes arm drift DOWN with pronation due to gravity and loss of UMN antigravity support. Arm drifting UPWARD is physiologically impossible with organic weakness — there is no muscle that could produce upward drift with hemiparesis, and it requires active motor effort to push upward.
POSITIVE Hoover sign: Left hip extension 5/5 with right leg contralateral flexion resistance.
Strength with distraction: Left arm strength improves from 2/5 to 4/5 when asked to count backwards from 100.

output.impression: Upward arm drift observed in the affected limb during the arm-drop test, a pattern inconsistent with the biomechanics of organic upper motor neuron weakness. Give-way weakness pattern and strength improvement with attentional distraction also documented. Clinical correlation recommended.

key_reasoning_points: IMMEDIATE GLUCOSE MEASUREMENT is the first priority in any T1DM patient with acute neurological symptoms — hypoglycemia is treatable in minutes and must be excluded before proceeding

ARM DRIFT TEST — arm drifting UPWARD is pathognomonic for functional motor disorder; it is physiologically impossible with organic weakness (no muscle can produce upward drift with hemiparesis) and requires active motor effort
Celiac disease has real neurological complications (gluten ataxia, neuropathy, B12 malabsorption) that must be specifically excluded with serology and nutritional testing before FND diagnosis
Young T1DM patient — vascular risk is low but not zero; DWI MRI provides definitive exclusion of stroke
